newsitem.title: FINLAND: UPM CEO sees pulp price falling near term.
newsitem.headline: UPM CEO sees pulp price falling near term.

text.p: Europe's biggest forest industry group UPM-Kymmene Oy's CEO Juha Niemela said on Tuesday he expected the price of pulp to go on falling in the near term at the current pace of a few dollars per month.
"The (pulp) price has crept downwards by a dollar or two per month, this kind of trend will probably continue in the next few months," Niemela told a news conference.

But despite the weakening pulp prices, UPM was in talks about raising fine paper prices by 10 percent. "It is a hike of about 10 percent, negotiations are underway, but we cannot yet see how much we will end up with," Niemela said.
The demand outlook for fine paper was the chief reason for UPM's view that a price hike could be feasible despite the ongoing pulp price fall, he said.

"The first possibilities for (pulp) price increases will come, I think, when the Canadians reduce their output in spring ... and when simultaneously seasonal demand picks up here at home as well as elsewhere in the world, particularly in China," Niemela said.
"But I don't belive at all in any rapid pulp price increase," he added.
On Monday, Suomen Optioporssi (SOP), a Finnish options exchange, said the value of northern bleached softwood pulp fell to $539.34 per tonne from $540.85 a week earlier.
In February, the mean pulp price calculated by SOP was $546.59, down from $556.86 in January and $559.05 in December.

UPM-Kymmene earlier said weaker prices and demand, mainly for pulp and fine paper, had dented 1996 earnings. By spring last year, pulp prices were just half of the peak levels in October 1995, UPM said in a statement with its 1996 results. @
"Better demand early in 1997 has raised capacity utilisation rates and paved the way for an increase in sales prices," UPM said in the statement.
"It is hoped to raise fine paper and LWC prices during the first quarter of the year," the company added.
Economic growth was expected to increase gradually in Europe, the company's main market, and this would increase paper consumption, UPM said.
